response.complaint_restatement: Sasha objects that the ‘higher-probability’ principle (PR1), which tells Ellis to give the blanket to Rowan, condemns her to certain death even though a feasible alternative would leave her with a better-than-even (60 %) chance to live.  From her standpoint the principle seems to treat her as a mere statistical loss for only a 20-percentage-point gain for Rowan.  The alternative principle (PR2) would instead give the blanket to Sasha, spare her the certainty of death, and leave Rowan facing an 80 % risk rather than certain death.  Sasha therefore claims that PR1 is not justifiable to her.
conceded_points: Under PR1 Sasha would indeed face certain death.
Under PR2 her ex-ante survival chance would be 60 %.
The numerical difference in lost chance (80 % vs 60 %) is only one way to compare complaints and does not on its own answer whether certainty of death is a distinct qualitative burden.
response.priority_premise: (NP1)   When two principles each leave one person to die, the person who would lose the larger ex-ante survival probability under a principle has the stronger ground for reasonable rejection, other things equal.
response.answer:
Why should Sasha accept NP1 despite bearing the worst outcome under PR1?

1.  Symmetry of the qualitative burden.
    •  No principle available can avoid imposing certainty of death on someone; the qualitative burden (‘certain death’) is therefore unavoidably symmetrical.  What a principle controls is who must bear it and how large a chance each person has of being spared.  Consequently, what distinguishes the two principles is each person’s ex-ante prospect, not whether certainty is imposed at all.  Focusing on comparative loss of chance is therefore an appropriate contractualist tie-breaker once the qualitative burden is inevitable.

2.  A personal reason every generic stranded hiker can endorse ex ante.
    •  Imagine an initially anonymous ‘position of stranded hiker’.  Before learning whether she is Sasha or Rowan, a person in that position has a higher personal reason to favour PR1 because it offers an 80 % prospect of survival to whoever ultimately occupies Rowan’s role, compared with 60 % to the other role.  Since each person could have found herself in either role, a principle that gives the higher prospect to whichever role has the higher baseline chance is harder for any person to reasonably reject.

3.  Comparative strength of rejection.
    •  Under PR2 Rowan would lose an 80-percentage-point chance to live; under PR1 Sasha loses 60.  Because both face the same qualitative harm if they lose, the greater quantitative loss gives Rowan a complaint that no one in Sasha’s position could reasonably insist on overriding.  To insist would be to claim that a 60-point loss is intolerable while an 80-point loss is acceptable—a claim that cannot be justified to the person asked to bear that larger loss.

4.  Why counting probabilities is licensed.
    •  Contractualism does not aggregate across persons, but it does allow each person to appeal to the magnitude of her own prospective loss when assessing justifiability.  Probabilities are an accepted currency for describing how serious that personal loss is when outcomes are uncertain.  Using them to compare two individuals’ complaints is therefore consistent with the framework so long as we do not sum or maximise overall survival.

5.  Remaining burden on Sasha.
    •  The defended rule still asks Sasha to accept certain death in the actual case—an undeniably grave burden.  What the justification claims is only that, given the symmetrical inevitability of one certain death, her demand to be spared at Rowan’s greater expense is not one that others in a like position must reasonably accept.
response.countercomplaint_to_alternative: Under PR2 Rowan can protest: “I am forced from an 80 % chance to certain death so that someone else may move from certain death to a 60 % chance.  My loss (80 points) is larger than the gain secured for Sasha (60 points), and I am singled out to bear it.”
response.comparative_justification: Both principles leave exactly one person dead; the decisive comparison is who is asked to surrender the larger ex-ante chance of survival.  Because Rowan’s prospective loss under PR2 (80 %) exceeds Sasha’s under PR1 (60 %), PR2 is subject to a rejection no less reasonable—and indeed stronger—than Sasha’s rejection of PR1.  Therefore PR1 remains the least-rejectable principle.

Each person can appeal to the size of her own survival-chance loss when assessing whether a principle is reasonably rejectable.
Larger personal losses constitute stronger grounds for reasonable rejection, other things equal.

conclusion.rationale: Action A (blanket to Rowan) remains provisionally preferred as supported by the least reasonably rejectable principle once symmetrical inevitability of one death is recognised and comparative loss of chance is weighed.

response.remaining_objection: Whether an 80 % vs 60 % comparison by itself always overrides a person’s appeal to avoid certainty of death remains contestable; some may hold that once chances exceed a certain threshold, removing all hope is qualitatively worse than reducing a high chance.
response.reversal_condition: If the survival probabilities were closer (e.g., 75 % vs 70 %) or reversed (Sasha 80 %, Rowan 60 %), the magnitude comparison would no longer clearly favour PR1 and Sasha’s complaint might then be strongest, shifting the decision.
